science.title: Parallel feature fusion networks for rotating machinery fault diagnosis with multi-sensor information
science.description: Rotating machinery constitutes fundamental components within vital industrial systems, including power generation and transport networks, where accurate malfunction detection is crucial for upholding the safety and efficiency of operations. Multi-sensor data fusion serves as a crucial strategy to improve diagnostic accuracy. However, effectively fusing heterogeneous sensor information still poses challenges. This is mainly attributed to the inadequate exploration of physical correlations between sensors and the limited integration of spatio-temporal characteristics in practical industrial scenarios. To overcome these limitations, this study introduces an innovative parallel feature fusion framework for fault diagnosis of industrial rotating machinery with heterogeneous multi-sensor data. The framework adopts a dual-branch feature extraction strategy: (i) a physics-informed graph isomorphism network that captures spatial and physical correlations among sensors, and (ii) a network constructed by global attention bidirectional gated recurrent unit that extracts global temporal patterns from real-world sensor time series. A cross-attention module is then employed to achieve synergistic fusion of spatial and temporal features. Extensive testing on industrial datasets confirms the approach’s efficacy, highlighting its applicability for identifying faults in rotating machinery.

science.title: Utilising virtual environments to assess the visibility of fallow deer to human hunters
science.description: Visual detection of prey is a critical element of human hunting behaviour. We examine how factors such as prey coat colouration, distance to the observer and orientation influence the ability of humans to visually locate fallow deer in simulated virtual environments. The simulated environment is a deciduous broad-leaved woodland that corresponds to the vegetation in interglacial Northwest Europe during the middle to late Pleistocene. We conducted two online target-present/absent visual search experiments (Experiment 1: N = 100, 16,800 trials; Experiment 2: N = 107, 19,268 trials). Results indicate that while the dappled coat colouration most commonly found in nature may confer advantages for avoiding detection beyond those caused by increased distance to the observer, it does not represent the most difficult-to-locate colouration among the variants investigated (dappled, dark, and albino). Our findings reveal that deer presented in lateral or oblique (45-degree) orientations are significantly easier to locate than those presented head-on. A principal factor potentially underlying this effect is that lateral and oblique views preserve the prototypical shape of the deer, whereas the head-on orientation may obscure these defining features. This is discussed regarding findings of proposed hunting lesions on bones in the archaeological record. This suggests that the lesions were mostly caused by projectiles targeting deer at lateral or oblique orientations to the hunter, which is consistent with our results.
